idiom_name: injected sync.Locker (sync.Mutex or sync.RWMutex.RLocker()) with defer as the scoped release
implementation_notes: The classic abstract Lock Strategy collapses into a two-method interface: sync.Locker is satisfied by sync.Mutex, by sync.RWMutex's RLocker() (the read-side policy) and by a hand-written no-op type, so the component stores a sync.Locker field and the composition root decides which policy it receives. Scoped Locking becomes mu.Lock(); defer mu.Unlock(), which releases on every return path without a guard class, and constructor injection (or functional options) replaces the template parameter. Keep the strategy an interface or a pointer - embedding a mutex in a struct means assignment copies lock state, which the go vet copylocks check flags - and remember that sync.Mutex.TryLock exists but offers no owner tracking, so a non-re-entrant mutex is the default policy.
pitfalls: Copying a struct that contains a mutex copies the lock state (go vet's copylocks check); hold the strategy as an interface or pointer and never pass a lock-owning component by value.
RLocker() grants only the read side, so using it as a component's write policy turns a reader/writer lock into a read-only one, and neither Mutex nor RWMutex is re-entrant - nested locking deadlocks.
defer inside a loop keeps every lock until the function returns, and only the race detector (go test -race) actually proves that a no-op or lock-free policy is safe for a given component.
